explain.say: Look at the dishes on rooftops from Cairo to São Paulo. Why are they all curved in the same way, with a little arm sticking out in front? Look at the first reason: a TV satellite is 36000 kilometres away, so its signals arrive as straight, side-by-side rays.

explain.say: Here is the magic of a parabola. Every ray coming in straight bounces to the very same point, called the focus. Look at the third reason. A flat plate or a ball shape could not do this exactly. Can you guess what sits at the focus?

faq.a: The curve is a parabola, which reflects all rays arriving straight on to one point. That collects a weak signal from the whole dish into one strong spot.

faq.q: What is the focus of a parabola?
faq.a: The special point inside the curve where all rays arriving parallel to its axis meet after bouncing. For y equals x squared, the focus is at 0, one quarter.
asks: Where is the focus of y = x^2?

faq.q: How does a parabolic dish collect signals?
faq.a: Each part of the dish catches a bit of the signal and reflects it to the focus, where the receiver sits. All those bits add up to a strong signal.
asks: How does a satellite dish work?

faq.q: Why not use a round, ball-shaped dish?
faq.a: A ball shape reflects rays to slightly different points, so the signal blurs. Only a parabola sends every parallel ray to exactly one point.
The bulb sits at the focus of a parabolic mirror. Light bouncing off the mirror leaves in parallel rays, making a strong beam.
asks: Why do torches have curved mirrors?

facts: A parabola reflects all rays parallel to its axis through its focus.
The parabola y = x²/(4f) has its focus at (0, f); for y = x² the focus is at (0, ¼).
